binders: A fixed probability space (Omega, Sigma, P).
An exponent p in the endpoint-inclusive range [1,infinity].
Real-valued random variables X (and, for vector-space or triangle-inequality assertions, X and Y) on Omega belonging to Lp.
hypotheses: The probability space (Omega, Sigma, P) is fixed.
Membership X in Lp means that X is a random variable on Omega with finite ||X||_Lp.
For finite p, ||X||_Lp is (E|X|^p)^(1/p); for p = infinity it is ess sup |X|.
conclusions: For every p in [1,infinity], the quantity ||.||_Lp is a norm on Lp.
For every p in [1,infinity], Lp is complete under this norm, hence is a Banach space.
definitions_and_conventions: Expectation E X is the Lebesgue integral of the real-valued random variable X : Omega -> R.
For fixed p and (Omega, Sigma, P), Lp is the vector space of all random variables X on Omega with finite Lp quantity.
The notation [1,infinity] includes the separately defined endpoint p = infinity.
implicit_context: Random variables are real-valued, as stated in the Section 1.1 footnote describing X : Omega -> R.
Vector addition and scalar multiplication are the standard operations on random variables.

To make the displayed Lp quantity positive definite and the resulting space literally normed, the conventional Lp identification of random variables equal almost surely is required, although the selected pages do not state that quotient explicitly.

details: The claim includes p = infinity, using essential supremum rather than the finite-p moment formula.
The claim is not restricted to 1 < p < infinity or to finite p.
The source explicitly calls ||.||_Lp a norm, not merely a seminorm or quasi-norm.
Minkowski's inequality (1.4) is cited for the triangle inequality.

The immediately following contrast says that for p < 1 the triangle inequality fails and the Lp quantity is not a norm; this contrast marks the lower boundary but is not an additional conclusion of the selected positive claim.
Banach space means that the normed vector space Lp is complete in the metric induced by ||.||_Lp.
Completeness is a separate required conclusion in addition to the norm axioms.
The source describes Lp as consisting of real-valued random variables on a fixed probability space.
Essential-supremum and expectation quantities are insensitive to almost-sure equality.
The customary almost-sure quotient is therefore semantically consequential for the word 'norm'.
The next paragraph says L2 is also a Hilbert space, but that stronger p = 2 specialization is context and is not part of the selected general Lp Banach claim.

undebatable_constraints: The probability space (Omega, Sigma, P) is fixed before forming Lp.
Lp consists of real-valued random variables with finite stated Lp quantity.
The quantified exponent range is all p in [1,infinity], including both endpoints.
For finite p the quantity is (E|X|^p)^(1/p), while p = infinity uses ess sup |X|.
The selected result asserts both that ||.||_Lp is a norm and that Lp is a Banach space.
The completeness assertion must not be reduced to Minkowski's triangle inequality or to normhood alone.

ambiguities.issue: The source calls Lp a vector space of random variables but does not explicitly say that random variables equal almost surely are identified.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF pages 1-2 (printed pages 5-6) define expectation, essential supremum, and Lp using random variables as functions, then call ||.||_Lp a norm; no quotient by almost-sure equality appears in the selected or immediately surrounding text.
ambiguities.impact: Read literally with pointwise equality of functions, nonzero functions supported on null sets have Lp quantity zero, so the quantity is only a seminorm and the norm/Banach claim is false as stated. The standard source meaning is therefore presumably the usual almost-sure equivalence-class Lp space, but that identification is inherited convention rather than explicit text here.

ambiguities.issue: The sentence 'This fact follows from Minkowski's inequality' compresses the justification for a two-part claim.
ambiguities.evidence: PDF page 2 (printed page 6) attributes normhood and Banach structure to Minkowski, while equation (1.4) in Section 1.2 supplies the triangle inequality but does not itself state or prove completeness.
ambiguities.impact: The explicit Banach-space assertion remains part of the contract; the citation to Minkowski should not be interpreted as weakening the claim to the triangle inequality or normhood only.

contract_plain_english: Fix a probability space and let Lp be the real-valued random variables with finite Lp size, using (E|X|^p)^(1/p) for finite p and essential supremum for p = infinity. For every p from 1 through infinity, this size is a norm and the resulting normed space is complete, hence Banach. The conventional identification of random variables that agree almost surely is needed for literal normhood, although the source does not explicitly state that quotient on these pages.
